name: GRIPP Golf Injury-Prevention Warm-up
whoItsFor: Golfers aged 45+ (and anyone else) who want a short, club-only warm-up they can do beside the first tee without mats or bands.
howToRun: Do it before every round or practice session - the trial asked players to use it at least twice a week.
Use a short iron (7-9 iron) as your prop and move slowly and with control.
Ten reps of each move on each side; the whole thing takes 5-10 minutes.
Stop any exercise that hurts. The trial was designed to test injury prevention, so don't treat it as proven protection.
description: Six standing exercises with a short iron, built by Dutch physios, sports doctors and the Dutch Golf Federation for an injury-prevention trial in golfers over 45.

exercises.name: Leg Swing (club at your side for support)
Arms in the Air (club overhead, arms straight)
Arm Rotations (club vertical, rotate each way)
Powerful Rotation (club low to high diagonal)

credit: Gladdines S, von Gerhardt AL, Verhagen E, Beumer A, Eygendaal D (Amphia Hospital, Amsterdam UMC, Erasmus MC, Dutch Golf Federation) - BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation 2022
sourceNote: Open-access trial protocol, CC BY 4.0. Exercises and the '10 times each side, short iron' rule are from Figure 3 of the paper. This is the protocol paper; the trial's injury results are not reported in it.

name: Bodyweight-Potentiated Golf Warm-up
whoItsFor: Competent golfers who warm up on the range and want a research-tested routine that finishes with jumps and plyo push-ups to wake up speed before driving.
howToRun: Use it before range sessions or rounds where you want to swing hard.
Work through the four blocks in order: raise (skipping), activate and mobilise, golf shots from wedge to driver, then the jumps and push-ups.
Rest about one minute after the last jump set before hitting your first full-effort drive.
Tested on 13 skilled male college golfers; it raised clubhead speed and carry in that study, but results in other golfers may differ.
description: The standardised RAMP warm-up from a St Mary's University study, with the bodyweight potentiation block (countermovement jumps and plyometric push-ups) that increased clubhead speed versus a normal warm-up.
credit: Bliss A, Livingstone H, Tallent J (St Mary's University, Twickenham) - Journal of Sport and Exercise Science 2021
sourceNote: Free-to-read journal article (Sport and Exercise Science New Zealand). Protocol from Table 1 (standardised warm-up + BWP condition). No licence or reuse restriction stated on the PDF or article page.

name: Utah Health Golf Program - Day 1 Strength & Mobility
series: University of Utah Health Golf Program
whoItsFor: Amateur golfers of any handicap who want a simple three-day strength, mobility and power plan with dumbbells, a band and a med ball.
howToRun: Three days a week (e.g. Mon/Wed/Fri), doing Day 1, 2 and 3 in order.
Start every session with the 5-10 minute warm-up.
Strength: 3 sets of 8-10 with a weight that leaves 1-2 reps in reserve; power: 2-3 sets of 5-8 done fast with full rest.
Progress by adding weight, reps or a set when it feels easy; keep it up 2-3 times a week through the season.
description: Full-body dumbbell strength plus hip and thoracic-spine mobility - the two areas the clinic says golfers most need for rotation.

exercises.name: Warm-up: Arm Wings with Torso Rotations

credit: Shane Thoreson, DPT, Golf Clinic physical therapist (University of Utah Health)
sourceNote: Free article on healthcare.utah.edu. Exercise names, sets and reps from the article; where a block gives no set count (mobility, balance) one set is stored, and session length is a Somax estimate. No reuse restriction found in the linked university disclaimer.

name: Concurrent Training for Golfers - Phase 1 Max Strength
whoItsFor: Experienced, well-trained golfers (the study used elite 16-year-old male players) who already lift and want a periodised in-season strength-to-power block.
howToRun: Two sessions a week (the study used Wednesday and Friday) for six weeks per phase: Phase 1, then 2, then 3.
In the study, sessions done before golf practice gave better jump, ball-speed and rotational-power results than the same sessions after practice.
Percentages are of your one-rep max; rest 4 minutes between sets.
Only for lifters with good technique - get coached if %1RM training is new to you.
description: Heavy 3x5 at 80% across five machine and free-weight lifts after a golf-specific movement block.
credit: Redondo JC, de Benito AM, Izquierdo JM, Garcia-Ramos A - PeerJ 2020
sourceNote: Open-access study, CC BY 4.0. Loads and sets from Table 2 (three six-week phases); the 10-min warm-up and 30-min individual functional block are described in the methods but not itemised.

name: TOGU Golf Core & Balance - Week 1
whoItsFor: Mid-handicap golfers (the study used 15-20 handicappers) who want a four-week core and balance block using balance discs and cushions.
howToRun: Three sessions a week, about 60 minutes, alongside normal golf practice.
Week 1 uses the foundation session; weeks 2-4 use the progression session.
Do a 10-minute warm-up before and a 10-minute cool-down after each session, as the study did.
In the study this improved FMS scores, balance and swing measures over four weeks; small sample (16 trained players).
description: Foundation week: four-round timed core holds and back extensions, with an unstable-surface plank.
credit: Li M, Ruan C, Zhang L (Shenzhen University) - Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology 2024
sourceNote: Open-access study, CC BY 4.0. Exercises and sets x time from Table 1 (TOGU Balanza disc and Dynair air cushion are the brand-name kit used).

description: Progression weeks: single-leg and two-foot balance on discs, med-ball holds and throws, rope rotations and anti-rotation on a cushion.

name: NHS Physio-Based Pilates (Leicestershire)
whoItsFor: People new to Pilates, including those with everyday back niggles, who want the gentle standing, lying and stretching routine NHS physios teach in class.
howToRun: The leaflet's dose is 8-12 reps of each exercise, 2 or 3 times a day - choose the exercises that suit you; a full run-through is about 25 minutes.
Set up each move with the five elements: breathing, centring, ribcage, shoulder blades, head and neck. Breathe out on the effort, never hold your breath.
Hold each stretch about 15-30 seconds.
The leaflet itself notes Pilates isn't proven better than other exercise for pain - pick what you enjoy, and ask a physio if anything hurts.
description: An NHS physiotherapy Pilates sequence: standing knee bends and heel raises, lying table-top and leg slides, bridge, side-lying leg work, prone swan and swimming, then six stretches.
credit: Leicestershire Partnership NHS Trust MSK Physiotherapy (leaflet 608)
sourceNote: Free NHS patient leaflet ('Your guide to physiotherapy based Pilates'). Exercise names, reps and hold times only. No reproduction restriction stated in the leaflet.

name: NHS Sitting Exercises
whoItsFor: Older adults, people returning after illness and anyone who finds standing or floor exercise hard - all done from a solid chair without arms.
howToRun: At least twice a week; combine with the NHS flexibility, balance and strength routines.
Use a stable chair without wheels or arms, feet flat and knees at right angles.
Build up the repetitions gradually over time.
Check with a GP first if you're unsure the exercises are right for you.
description: Five gentle seated moves for the chest, upper back, hips, ankles and neck.
sourceNote: Information from the NHS website is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0. Exercise names and reps only.

name: NHS Post-Workout Stretch
whoItsFor: Anyone finishing a run, walk, gym session or class who wants a quick, gentle cool-down for the legs and hips.
howToRun: After every workout, once your breathing has settled.
Hold each stretch 15-20 seconds per side; spend longer if you need to.
Stretch to mild tension only and keep breathing.
Injured, pregnant or have a medical condition? Ask a physio which stretches suit you.
description: Five stretches for the buttocks, hamstrings, inner thighs, calves and front of thighs, about five minutes in total.
sourceNote: Information from the NHS website is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0. Exercise names and hold times only.

name: NHS Low Back Pain Gentle Exercises (Berkshire)
whoItsFor: People with everyday (non-serious) low back pain or stiffness who want four gentle moves to do little and often.
howToRun: Twice a day, morning and afternoon, building from 1 up to 20 repetitions.
Some discomfort is OK, but the moves shouldn't make your symptoms much worse.
Keep up your normal activities - long bed rest slows recovery.
Red flags (new bladder or bowel problems, numbness in the saddle area, worsening leg weakness) need urgent medical help, not exercise.
description: Knee rolls, knees to chest, bridge and standing side bends from an NHS physiotherapy leaflet.
credit: Berkshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust Physiotherapy (leaflet BH1165n)
sourceNote: Free NHS patient leaflet, reviewed Feb 2026. Exercise names and rep ranges only. No reproduction restriction stated in the leaflet.

name: LiveLighter 5x5x5 Office Worker Routine
whoItsFor: Desk workers who want a five-minute stretch break they can do from their chair at work.
howToRun: Five minutes, five times a week - for example once each workday.
Sit tall with feet flat; move slowly into each position.
Hold each stretch for the time shown and breathe normally.
Pair it with regular standing or walking breaks through the day.
description: Australian public-health routine: neck, ankles, hips, torso and shoulders, all seated.
sourceNote: Free downloadable LiveLighter mobility guide. Exercise names and holds only. No reuse restriction stated on the guide; site terms page could not be located.

name: 10 Stretches to Do as You Age
whoItsFor: Older adults who want a full-body stretching routine using a chair, wall and towel, with standing, seated and lying options.
howToRun: Twice a week, after a few minutes of walking or after strength or endurance exercise - not before.
Hold each stretch 10-30 seconds and repeat 3-5 times (the lower number is shown); never bounce.
A mild pull is fine; sharp pain means ease off.
Had hip, back or other surgery? Check with your doctor first.
description: Ten classic stretches originally published by the US National Institutes of Health: thighs, calves, back, shoulders, hamstrings, ankles, hips, neck, chest and lower back.

exercises.name: Seated Ankle Stretch (toes up, toes away)
Lying Hip Stretch (knee out to side)

credit: Emory Healthy Aging Study (Emory University), exercises sourced from the US National Institutes of Health
sourceNote: Free PDF. Its exercises are credited to NIH (US federal public-domain material). Where a 3-5 rep range is given, 3 sets are stored.
